paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 3
p: וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים.
And it came to pass at the end of two full years.
הָעִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה יוֹסֵף בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר תְּחִילָּה עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִתּוֹסַף לוֹ עוֹד שְׁנַיִם,
The reason why Joseph was imprisoned first for ten years and afterward had two more years added to his sentence
כִּי תְּחִלָּה נִגְזַר עָלָיו עֶשֶׂר יַעַן כִּי חָטָא נֶגֶד עֲשָׂרָה שְׁבָטִים
is because initially ten years were decreed upon him for having sinned in speaking ill of the ten tribes (his brothers),
וְאַחַר כָּךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר נִתְבָּרֵר בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר אָז נִתּוֹסַף לוֹ עוֹד שְׁנַיִם נֶגֶד עַצְמוֹ וְנֶגֶד בִּנְיָמִין,
and afterward, once he had been purified of that in prison during the ten years, two additional years were added corresponding to himself and his full brother Benjamin (making twelve in all);
כִּי כָּךְ הוּא הַמִּדָּה כַּאֲשֶׁר יֶחֱטָא הָאָדָם נֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז יְבִיאֵהוּ הַשֵּׁם לְבֵרוּרִים אֲשֶׁר הָאָדָם יִסְבּוֹל מֵהֶם,
for such is the divine attribute: when a person sins against Hashem, blessed be He, Hashem brings him into purifying trials from which the person suffers;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתְבָּרֵר לְטוֹב וְיִתְכַּפֵּר אָז צָרִיךְ לִסְבּוֹל מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ
and afterward, once he has been clarified for the good and achieved atonement for the original flaw, he still needs to undergo a final purification for the very fact that he had to suffer—
כִּי לָמָּה הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְהַכְנִיס עַצְמוֹ בְּדָבָר הַצָּרִיךְ בֵּרוּר וְיֻצְרַךְ לִסְבּוֹל מִזֶּה
namely, why did he cause himself to enter into a situation requiring painful clarification so that he had to suffer from it?
כִּי מִמַּה שֶּׁהָאָדָם סוֹבֵל גַּם כִּבְיָכוֹל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ סוֹבֵל עִמּוֹ כִּי "בְּכָל צָרָתָם לוֹ צָר",
For whenever a person suffers, Hashem, blessed be He, as it were, suffers along with him, as it is written, "In all their affliction He is afflicted" (Isaiah 63:9);
וְלָכֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר יְבָרֵר הָאָדָם אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי חֶטְאוֹ, אָז נוֹסָף לָזֶה הַבֵּרוּר צָרִיךְ לְבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ גַּם עַל צַעֲרוֹ,

and therefore, after a person has purified himself in proportion to his original sin, in addition to that purification he must also purify himself for his own distress (and the distress of the Shechinah),
כִּי גַּם זֶה הוּא שֶׁמֶץ חֵטְא כְּמוֹ שֶׁמְּבוֹאָר בַּגְּמָרָא (תַּעֲנִית יוֹד אָלֶף עַמּוּד אָלֶף) אֲשֶׁר חָטָא שֶׁצִּיעֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ,

because causing oneself pain also carries a trace of sin, as is explained in the Gemara (Ta'anit 11a) regarding the Nazirite who brings a sin-offering "for having sinned against the soul" by afflicting himself;
לָכֵן בַּתְּחִילָּה נִגְזַר עַל יוֹסֵף עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים נֶגֶד עֲשָׂרָה אֶחָיו
therefore ten years were initially decreed upon Joseph corresponding to his ten brothers,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר נִתְבָּרֵר בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר כְּכֶסֶף צָרוּף בַּעֲלִיל, אָז הֻצְרַךְ לְהִתְבָּרֵר עַל צַעֲרוֹ וְעַל צַעַר בִּנְיָמִין אָחִיו
and afterward, once he had been refined in prison like silver smelted in a crucible, he still needed to undergo two years of clarification for his own anguish and the anguish of his brother Benjamin,
וְאַחַר שֶׁבֵּרֵר גַּם אֶת זֶה בְּאֵלּוּ הַשְּׁתֵּי שָׁנִים אָז מִיָּד נִפְדָּה.
and as soon as he completed that purification during those two additional years, he was immediately redeemed.
h:
Why Yosef Remained in Prison
The reason why Joseph was imprisoned first for ten years and afterward had two more years added to his sentence

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 4
p: וְהִנֵּה עֹמֵד עַל הַיְאֹר.
And behold, he stood over the Nile River.

אִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פֵּא טֵית, גִּימֶל) אָמַר פַּרְעֹה מִי מִתְקַיֵּים עַל מִי אֲנִי עַל אֱלֹהַי אוֹ אֱלֹהַי עָלַי, אָמַר לוֹ אַתָּה עַל אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְהִנֵּה עוֹמֵד עַל הַיְאוֹר".

It is stated in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 89:3): Pharaoh asked, "Who stands over whom—do I stand over my god (the Nile), or does my god stand over me?" God answered him: "You stand over your god, as it is stated, 'And behold, he stood over the Nile.'"
הָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּי פַּרְעֹה רָצָה לָדַעַת אַחֲרֵי רְאוֹתוֹ כִּי כֹל אֲשֶׁר יַחְפֹּץ יַצְלִיחַ,
The inner meaning of this is that Pharaoh—upon seeing that whatever he desired succeeded—wanted to know and fathom the root of his success:
רָצָה לַעֲמוֹד עַל הִתְבּוֹנְנוּת הַדָּבָר אִם אֱלֹהָיו וְיִרְאָתוֹ מוֹשְׁלִים עָלָיו וְלֹא יָבֹא לְמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר רַק מַה שֶּׁאֱלֹהָיו יִשְׁלַח לוֹ לְפִיכָךְ יַצְלִיחַ,

he wanted to understand whether his deity (the spiritual minister of Egypt) ruled over him such that nothing ever entered Pharaoh's mind except what his deity first projected into him, and that was why it succeeded,
אוֹ תְּחִילָּה יָבֹא לְמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ וְלִרְצוֹנוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת וְאַחַר כָּךְ אֱלֹהָיו וְכֹחוֹ עוֹזְרִים לוֹ לְהַצְלִיחַ,
or whether the initiative first arose in Pharaoh's own mind and will, and afterward his deity and planetary force assisted him to succeed;
וְאָמַר לוֹ אַתָּה עַל אֱלֹהֶיךָ, הַיְינוּ תְּחִילָּה יָבֹא לְמַחְשַׁבְתְּךָ וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַכֹּחַ הַמּוֹשֵׁל עָלָיו יֻכְרַח לְעוֹזְרְךָ.

and he was shown in his dream: "You stand over your god"—meaning that the initiative first arises in your own mortal thought, and afterward the spiritual force governing Egypt is compelled to assist you.
אֲבָל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ כֵן כִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם מֶרְכָּבָה לַשְּׁכִינָה וּכְפִי רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן יִתְנַהֲגוּ,
Among Israel, however, it is not so! For Israel are a chariot for the Divine Presence (Shechinah), and they conduct themselves solely according to His prior will, blessed be He—
רַק לֶעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיַּגִּיעוּ לְתַכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵמוּת אָז נֶאֱמַר (אִיּוֹב כָּף בֵּית, כָּף חֵית) "וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ".
only in the ultimate future, when they reach the pinnacle of perfection, is it stated of them (Job 22:28), "You shall decree a matter, and it shall be established for you."
וּכְמוֹ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אַחַר נִסָּיוֹן הָעֲשִׂירִי, וְיִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב כְּשֶׁנִּשְׁלְמוּ, עֲלֵיהֶם נֶאֱמַר (יְשַׁעְיָה נּוּן חֵית, יוֹד דָּלֶת) "אָז תִּתְעַנַּג עַל הַשֵּׁם".

And similarly regarding our father Abraham, peace be upon him, after he passed the tenth test, as well as Isaac and Jacob once they reached complete perfection, concerning them it is stated (Isaiah 58:14), "Then you shall delight over (al) Hashem."
וְזֶה נִרְמָז בַּגְּמָרָא (שַׁבָּת סָמֶךְ טֵית עַמּוּד בֵּית) הַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מָתַי שַׁבָּת
And this distinction is alluded to in the Gemara (Shabbat 69b): If one is traveling in a desert and does not know which day is Shabbat—
רַב הוּנָא אָמַר מוֹנֶה שִׁשָּׁה יָמִים וּמְשַׁמֵּר יוֹם אֶחָד, חִיָּיא בַּר רַב אוֹמֵר מְשַׁמֵּר יוֹם אֶחָד וּמוֹנֶה שִׁשָּׁה.
Rav Huna said: He counts six working days and then observes one day as Shabbat; whereas Chiyya bar Rav said: He first observes one day as Shabbat and then counts six days.
כִּי שֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הֵם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם וְשַׁבָּת הַיְינוּ הַסִּיַּעְתָּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
For the six working days represent human initiative and effort (hishtadlut), while Shabbat represents the divine assistance and illumination from Hashem, blessed be He;

וְרַב הוּנָא מְדַבֵּר בָּאָדָם שֶׁנִּשְׁלַם בַּכֹּל, שֶׁלִּבּוֹ נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז מֻתָּר לוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת וְאַחַר כָּךְ יְבַקֵּשׁ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּגְמוֹר בַּעֲדוֹ,

and Rav Huna speaks of a person who has reached complete perfection, whose heart is naturally drawn after the will of Hashem, blessed be He—such a person may first initiate effort ("count six days") and afterward pray that Hashem, blessed be He, crown his effort with completion ("observe one day");
אֲבָל בְּעוֹד שֶׁאֵין הָאָדָם בִּשְׁלֵמוּת אָז צָרִיךְ לְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם קוֹדֵם כָּל מַעֲשֶׂה, וְאִם יַסְכִּים לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז יַעֲשֶׂה.

whereas Chiyya bar Rav speaks of a person who has not yet reached complete perfection: he must first nullify his will and accept the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven prior to any action ("first observe one day"), and only if Hashem, blessed be He, grants His assent may he then proceed to act ("and then count six").
h:
Pharaoh at the Nile and the Nature of Power
3): Pharaoh asked, "Who stands over whom—do I stand over my god (the Nile), or does my god stand over me?" God answered him: "You stand over your god, as it…

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 5
p: וַיִּשְׁלַח פַּרְעֹה וְכוּלֵי וַיְרִיצֻהוּ מִן הַבּוֹר.
Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they rushed him (vayeritzuhu) out of the dungeon.
הַיְינוּ שֶׁנִּתְרַצָּה עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָבַר עָלָיו,
The word vayeritzuhu (from the root ratzoh, conciliation) indicates that Joseph became completely conciliated and at peace with everything he had endured,
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שָׁלַח שִׂמְחָה בְּלִבּוֹ לְבַל יִהְיֶה לוֹ שׁוּם תַּרְעוֹמוֹת עָלָיו.
because Hashem, blessed be He, sent such joy into his heart that he harbored no lingering grievance whatsoever over his past suffering.
h:
Yosef Is Hurried from the Dungeon
The word vayeritzuhu (from the root ratzoh, conciliation) indicates that Joseph became completely conciliated and at peace with everything he had endured

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
p: תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אוֹתוֹ.
You can hear (understand) a dream to interpret it.
הַיְינוּ כִּי כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵם כַּחֲלוֹם הַצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן
That is, all the affairs and pleasures of this physical world are like a dream that requires interpretation,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּפְתּוֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם כֵּן יָקוּם אֶצְלוֹ,
and just as a dream follows its interpretation (Berakhot 55b), so too whatever meaning a person gives to his worldly experiences is what they become for him!
וְהָאָדָם הַמֵּבִין בַּכֹּל כִּי הַכֹּל הוּא רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְרַק מִמּוֹצָא פִיו יִחְיֶה הַכֹּל, זֶה מֵבִין טַעַם בְּכָל דָּבָר וּמַגִּיעַ לְחַיִּים אֲמִיתִּיִּים,

Thus, a person who understands in every worldly matter that everything comes solely from Hashem, blessed be He, and that everything lives only by the utterance of His mouth, perceives the inner spiritual taste in everything and attains true, eternal life;
כְּמוֹ לֶחֶם הָעִיקָּר הַמְחַיֶּה הַנִּמְצָא בּוֹ הוּא הַמּוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם

for instance, with bread: the primary life-force within it is the utterance of the mouth of Hashem ("man does not live by bread alone, but by every utterance of the mouth of Hashem," Deuteronomy 8:3),
וּמִי שֶׁאוֹכֵל פָּשׁוּט כִּבְהֵמָה, אֵינוֹ מַשִּׂיג מֵהַלֶּחֶם רַק חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
so one who eats it coarsely like an animal—"interpreting" it as mere physical matter—derives from the bread nothing more than transient, physical life,
וְהַמֵּבִין כִּי מוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמְחַיֶּה זֶה יַשִּׂיג חַיֵּי עוֹלָם,
whereas one who understands and "interprets" while eating that the divine utterance of Hashem's mouth is what gives life will attain eternal life through that very bread!
כִּי לֶחֶם הוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת חֲלֹם הַיְינוּ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן,
For the Hebrew word lechem (לֶחֶם — bread) has the exact same letters as chalom (חֲלֹם — dream), teaching that bread is like a dream that depends on how one interprets it;
וְכֵן הוּא כָּל הֲנָאוֹת, כִּי כָּל הַהֲנָאוֹת וְהַטּוֹבוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם נִמְשָׁלִין לְלֶחֶם.
and the same applies to all worldly pleasures, for all the delights and goods of this world are exemplified by bread.
h:
The Interpretation of Dreams and the Illusion of This World
That is, all the affairs and pleasures of this physical world are like a dream that requires interpretation

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 7
p: וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה אֶת שֵׁם יוֹסֵף צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ.
And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Tzafnat Pa'neach.
פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י כִּי מִלַּת פַּעְנֵחַ אֵין לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן בַּמִּקְרָא,
Rashi explained that the word Pa'neach has no parallel anywhere in Scripture.
וְיֵרָאֶה כִּי פַּרְעֹה הָיָה רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר פּוֹתֵחַ אַךְ לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהוֹצִיא מִשְּׂפָתָיו אֵלּוּ הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, הַיְינוּ וָא"ו וְתָי"ו,

And it appears that Pharaoh actually wanted to say Tzafnat Pote'ach (פּוֹתֵחַ — "Unlocker of hidden things"), but he was spiritually unable to utter those two middle letters, Vav (ו) and Tav (ת), from his lips:
כִּי אוֹת וָא"ו מְרַמֵּז עַל חַיִּים וְאוֹת תָי"ו הוּא חוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֱמֶת,
because the letter Vav alludes to true Life, and the letter Tav is the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, Emet (Truth),
וּבְאֵלּוּ הָאוֹתִיּוֹת אֵין לְהָאֻמּוֹת שׁוּם תְּפִיסָה כִּי אֵין לָהֶם חַיִּים אֲמִיתִּיִּים רַק לְפִי מַרְאִית הָעַיִן,
and the nations of the world have no grasp of these two letters, since they do not possess true, eternal life, but only superficial existence according to the appearance of the eye (עַיִן — Ayin);
וְלָכֵן אָמַר בִּמְקוֹמָם עַיִ"ן וְנוּ"ן.
and therefore, in place of Vav and Tav (in פּוֹתֵחַ), his tongue substituted the letters Ayin and Nun (producing פַּעְנֵחַ — spelling ayin, "eye").
h:
Tzafnas Paneach: Revealing What Is Hidden
Rashi explained that the word Pa'neach has no parallel anywhere in Scripture

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 8
p: וְאֵל שַׁדַּי יִתֵּן לָכֶם רַחֲמִים.
And may El Shaddai (God Almighty) grant you mercy.
פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י מִי שֶׁאָמַר לְעוֹלָמוֹ דַּי הוּא יֹאמַר לְצָרוֹתַי דַּי.
Rashi explained: "May He Who said to His universe 'Enough!' (Dai) say to my troubles 'Enough!'"
הָרַב הַקָּדוֹשׁ מִפְּשִׁיסְחָא אָמַר עַל שֵׁם שַׁדַּי,
The Holy Jew of Peshischa (the Yehudi HaKadosh) explained the divine Name Shaddai as follows:
כִּי כְּשֶׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם הָיָה מַרְחִיב וְהוֹלֵךְ כְּמַאֲמַר הַגְּמָרָא (חֲגִיגָה יוֹד בֵּית עַמּוּד אָלֶף) עַד שֶׁאָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא דַּי,
when the universe was created, it kept expanding and stretching without limit, as stated in the Gemara (Chagigah 12a), until the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked it and said "Enough! (Dai)";
וְהוּא כִּי עִיקַּר בְּרִיאוּת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה כְּדֵי שֶׁיּוּכַּר גְּדוּלָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלָכֵן אָמַר דַּי שֶׁמִּזֶּה יוּכַל לְהִוָּדַע,

and the meaning of this is that the primary purpose of creating the universe was so that His greatness, blessed be He, might be recognized through it, and therefore He said "Enough!"—meaning: "What has been created thus far is sufficient for My greatness to be known!"
וְזֶה שֶׁהִזְכִּיר יַעֲקֹב כָּאן זֶה הַשֵּׁם, הַיְינוּ כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵבִיא יִסּוּרִין עַל הָאָדָם כְּדֵי לְבָרְרוֹ שֶׁיַּכִּיר אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ,
And this is why Jacob invoked this specific Name (El Shaddai) here: because Hashem, blessed be He, brings tribulations upon a person solely to refine him so that he comes to recognize his Creator,
וְלָכֵן אָמַר זֶה הַשֵּׁם הוּא שֶׁיֹּאמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דַּי שֶׁמִּזֶּה שֶׁעָבַר עָלַי הִכַּרְתִּי הַכֹּל,

and therefore Jacob prayed with this Name, asking that Hashem, blessed be He, say "Enough!"—for "from all the troubles that have already passed over me, I have come to recognize everything You wished me to know!"
וּבֶאֱמֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי הָאָבוֹת לֹא הָיוּ מִצַּד עַצְמָם, רַק מִמַּה שֶׁהִשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן הִתְפַּלְּלוּ אֵלָיו, וְכָל תְּפִלָּתָם הָיָה בְּעִתּוֹ וּבִזְמַנּוֹ,

And in truth, none of the words of the Patriarchs were spoken merely on their own initiative; rather, they prayed to Hashem according to what Hashem, blessed be He, Himself inspired within them, so that every prayer of theirs was offered at its exact, divinely appointed moment—
כִּי כָאן הִסְכִּים הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֵאמֹר דַּי עַל כָּל צָרוֹתָיו,
for at this precise juncture Hashem, blessed be He, had indeed agreed in Heaven to say "Enough!" to all of Jacob's troubles,
וּכְמוֹ כֵן אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אַחַר נִסָּיוֹן הָעֲשִׂירִי הִתְחִיל לְבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא יְנַסֵּהוּ עוֹד,
just as our father Abraham, peace be upon him, only began to plead for mercy from Hashem, blessed be He, not to test him anymore after completing the tenth test (the Akeidah),
וְזֹאת הָיָה לְפִי שֶׁהוּסְכַּם אָז גַּם דַּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא יְנַסֶּנּוּ עוֹד.
because at that moment it had already been agreed in the mind of Hashem, blessed be He, not to test him any further.
h:
El Shaddai: Mercy Amidst Limitation
Rashi explained: "May He Who said to His universe 'Enough!' (Dai) say to my troubles 'Enough!'

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 9
p: מַה נֹּאמַר לַאדֹנִי מַה נְּדַבֵּר וְגוֹמֵר הָאֱלֹקִים מָצָא אֶת עֲוֹן עֲבָדֶיךָ.
What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak, or how shall we clear ourselves? God has found out the iniquity of your servants.
בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צָדִי בֵּית, טֵית) יוֹדְעִים אָנוּ שֶׁלֹּא גָּנַבְנוּ,
In the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 92:9) Judah says: "We know with certainty that we did not steal the goblet,"
הַיְינוּ בְּזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה יוֹדְעִים אָנוּ בְּבֵירוּר שֶׁאֵין בָּנוּ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ מֶנְהוּ,
meaning: regarding this specific accusation of stealing the silver cup, we know with absolute clarity that there is not the slightest trace of guilt in us;
רַק אַחַר כִּי אִנָּה הַשֵּׁם לְפָנֵינוּ מַעֲשֶׂה כָּזֶה בֶּטַח נִמְצָא בָּנוּ אֵיזֶה עִנְיָן כַּדּוֹמֶה.
however, since Hashem has orchestrated such a false accusation of theft against us, there must surely exist within us some analogous iniquity measure for measure!
וְהִיא שֶׁגָּנַבְנוּ דַּעַת אָבִינוּ בִּמְכִירַת יוֹסֵף, וּמִסִּיבַּת זֶה נִתְעוֹלֵל עָלֵינוּ מַעֲשֶׂה הַלֵּזוּ.
And that iniquity is that we stole our father's mind (deceived him) in the sale of Joseph, and because of that sin this ordeal has been brought upon us.
h:
Yehudah’s Confession Before Yosef
9) Judah says: "We know with certainty that we did not steal the goblet

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 1
p: וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָא.
Then Judah approached him.
זֶה שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב (שְׁמוּאֵל בֵּית כָּף גִּימֶל, גִּימֶל) "אָמַר אֱלֹקֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִי דִבֶּר צוּר יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹשֵׁל בָּאָדָם צַדִּיק מוֹשֵׁל יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים".
This is what Scripture states (II Samuel 23:3): "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: 'He who rules over man must be righteous, ruling in the fear of God.'"
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁבֵּיאֲרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מוֹעֵד קָטָן טֵית זַיִן עַמּוּד בֵּית) צַדִּיק מוֹשֵׁל בְּיִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים.
And as our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Moed Katan 16b): "The righteous one rules over the fear of God (i.e., I rule over man, but who rules over Me? The tzaddik!)."
"אָמַר אֱלֹקֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל", הַיְינוּ הַכְּלָלִים שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וְהֵם הָרְמַ"ח מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה וְשַׁסַּ"ה מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה אֲשֶׁר נִיתְּנוּ בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שָׁוֶה בְּשָׁוֶה.

"The God of Israel said" refers to the general principles of the words of Torah—namely, the 248 positive commandments (רְמַ"ח — 248) and the 365 negative commandments (שַׁסַּ"ה — 365) that were given equally to every soul in Israel.
"לִי דִבֶּר צוּר יִשְׂרָאֵל", לִי הַיְינוּ לְהַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, לָזֶה מְדַבֵּר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּפְרָט וְנוֹתֵן לוֹ תַּקּוּפוּת אַחַר חֶטְאוֹ

"To me spoke the Rock of Israel"—"to me" refers specifically to the penitent (ba'al teshuvah, exemplified by David and Judah): to such a person Hashem, blessed be He, speaks individually and grants him special fortitude after his sin,
שֶׁנִּדְמָה לוֹ כִּי אָפֵס תִּקְוָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְיָשׁוֹב אֶל הַשֵּׁם, אָז נוֹתֵן לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא תַּקּוּפוּת.
when it seems to him that all hope is lost for him and yet he returns to Hashem; then the Holy One, blessed be He, imbues him with fierce spiritual strength.
וְלָזֶה נִשְׁתַּנּוּ הַדְּבָרִים, כִּי בַּתְּחִילָה נֶאֱמַר "אָמַר" הַיְינוּ לָשׁוֹן רַכָּה, וְאֵצֶל הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה נֶאֱמַר "דִבֶּר" הַיְינוּ תַּקּוּפוּת,
And for this reason the wording shifts: initially it states "said" (amar), which is a soft expression, whereas regarding the penitent it states "spoke" (diber), which denotes strength and fortitude;
גַּם בַּתְּחִילָה נֶאֱמַר "אֱלֹקֵי" וְאַחַר כָּךְ נֶאֱמַר "צוּר" אֲשֶׁר הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְשׁוֹן תַּקּוּפוּת וְחִיזּוּק.
furthermore, initially it states "God of (Elokei)" and afterward it states "Rock of (Tzur)," which is likewise an expression of rock-solid fortitude and reinforcement.

"מוֹשֵׁל בָּאָדָם צַדִּיק" הַיְינוּ אִם הָיָה הַחֵטְא בְּדָבָר בִּגְזֵרַת חֲכָמִים עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר "מוֹשֵׁל בָּאָדָם צַדִּיק" הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹשֵׁל עֲלֵיהֶם, כִּי אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה.

"He rules over man, the righteous one" means that if the sin was against a rabbinic enactment (decreed by "man"), concerning this it is stated "the righteous one rules over man"—meaning that the penitent prevails over those decrees, for nothing stands in the way of repentance.
"מוֹשֵׁל יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים" הַיְינוּ אִם הָיָה הַחֵטְא נֶגֶד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר "מוֹשֵׁל יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים" הַיְינוּ שֶׁגַּם עַל זֶה יִמְשׁוֹל,

"Ruling in the fear of God" means that even if the sin violated the Written Torah itself, concerning this it is stated "ruling over the fear of God"—meaning that through repentance he prevails over this as well;
עַל הַכֹּל נֶאֱמַר (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הֵא עַמּוּד אָלֶף) "נְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר הוּקַם עָל" שֶׁהוּקַם עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה,
for over everything it is stated (Avodah Zarah 5a, on II Samuel 23:1), "The saying of the man raised on high (al)"—namely David, who raised up and established the yoke (ol) of repentance!
כִּי אַף שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה נִיתְּנוּ בְּיִרְאָה מוּפְלֶגֶת וְעַל כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים שֶׁאִיְּימוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה כַּיָּדוּעַ, זֹאת אֵינוֹ רַק לִפְנֵי הַחֵטְא נֶאֱמַר,

For although the words of Torah were given in tremendous awe, and regarding numerous transgressions our Sages, of blessed memory, issued dire warnings (that one who commits them cannot repent or forfeits his share), as is known, all of that was stated solely prior to the sin to deter a person;
אֲבָל נֶגֶד תְּשׁוּבָה אֵין לְךָ שׁוּם דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד, וּלְאַחַר שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לָאָדָם מִכְשׁוֹל לֹא יִתְיָאֵשׁ עַצְמוֹ כִּי לֹא יִשָּׁאֵר לֶעָתִיד שׁוּם חֵטְא עַל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל,

whereas once a person has stumbled, nothing whatsoever stands in the way of repentance, and after a stumbling occurs to a person he must never despair of himself, because in the ultimate future no sin at all will remain upon any soul of Israel;
וְעִיקַּר זֹאת הַתַּקּוּפוּת נִמְצָא בְּשֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָא,
and the primary root of this unyielding fortitude resides in the tribe of Judah;
עַל כֵּן "וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָא" אַף שֶׁלֹּא נִרְאֶה עַתָּה חֲדָשׁוֹת בִּדְבָרָיו, אַךְ שֶׁמַּרְאֶה בִּדְבָרָיו גוֹדֶל תְּקוּפָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר בְּלִי סָפֵק נִמְצָא עַתָּה צְמִיחַת יְשׁוּעָה.

therefore "Then Judah approached him"—even though on the surface no new legal arguments appear in his speech here, through his words he displayed the sheer magnitude of his spiritual fortitude and resolve, through which the sprouting of salvation was undoubtedly brought forth right then.
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ הַפָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כָּף דָּלֶת, כָּף אָלֶף) "יְרָא אֶת הַשֵּׁם בְּנִי וָמֶלֶךְ".
And this is the meaning of the verse (Proverbs 24:21): "Fear Hashem, my son, and the king; and do not meddle with them that are given to change (shonim)."
בְּנִי הַיְינוּ לְשׁוֹן בִּינָה וְהוּא שֶׁיְּהֵא יִרְאָתְךָ מְבוֹרֶרֶת וַאֲמִיתִּיּוֹת,
"My son (beni)" is an expression of understanding (binah), meaning that your fear of Heaven should be clarified and genuine;
"וָמֶלֶךְ" הַיְינוּ שֶׁתִּהְיֶה מֶלֶךְ וְתַקִּיף בְּבִטָּחוֹן גָּדוֹל בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
"and the king" means that you yourself should be like a king, fierce and resolute with great trust in Hashem, blessed be He;
"וְעִם שׁוֹנִים אַל תִּתְעָרָב", וְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (סוֹטָה כָּף בֵּית עַמּוּד אָלֶף) אֵלּוּ הַמּוֹרִים הֲלָכָה מִתּוֹךְ מִשְׁנָתָן,

"and do not meddle with shonim (those who repeat)"—and it is stated in the Gemara (Sotah 22a): This refers to those who issue halakhic rulings straight from their rote Mishnah (without understanding the underlying reasoning in the Gemara);
וּמַקְשֶׁה פְּשִׁיטָא וּמְשַׁנֵּי מַאן דְּאָמַר כְּרַב הוּנָא דְּאָמַר כָּל הָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה וְשָׁנָה בָּהּ הוּתְּרָה לוֹ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן,

and the Gemara asks: Why would one need to be warned against associating with someone who repeats a sin, which is obvious? And it answers that according to the one who explains shonim via Rav Huna's statement—"Whoever commits a transgression and repeats (shanah) it, it becomes permitted to him"—the verse teaches us
הַיְינוּ שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת נִמְצָא אֵיזֶה מָקוֹם גַּם לָזֶה כַּמְּבוֹאָר עַל פָּסוּק "וְיָד תִּהְיֶה לְךָ" [חֵלֶק אָלֶף תֵּצֵא],

that in truth, when a righteous person repeatedly feels compelled to do an act that appears questionable on the surface, there can be a hidden divine root to it, as is explained on the verse "And you shall have a place outside the camp" (Part One, Parashat Ki Teitzei);
וְזֶה הָיָה תַּקּוּפוּת יְהוּדָא אַחֲרֵי אֲשֶׁר אֵירַע לוֹ שֶׁאָמַר "אָנֹכִי אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ", וְעָבַר עַל מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר (יְבָמוֹת קוּף טֵית עַמּוּד בֵּית) "הַרְחֵק מִן הָעַרְבוּת"

and this was the fortitude of Judah: after it happened that he pledged "I will be surety for him (e'ervenu)"—seemingly violating the counsel of Solomon (Proverbs 24:21 / Yevamot 109b) "do not become a guarantor (al tit'arav)," and having already lost two sons and guaranteed Benjamin under a ban on both worlds—
וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן הָיָה בָּטוּחַ שֶׁיּוּצְמַח לוֹ הַיְשׁוּעָה.
nevertheless he remained unshakably confident that salvation would sprout for him!
h:
Vayigash: Yehudah Draws Near to Yosef
This is what Scripture states (II Samuel 23:3): "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: 'He who rules over man must be righteous, ruling in…

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 2
p: וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָא.
Then Judah approached him.
הִנֵּה זֶה הַכֹּחַ נָתַן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְיָאֵשׁ עַצְמוֹ לְעוֹלָם, אַף כִּי יִרְאֶה שֶׁיַּעֲבוֹר עָלָיו מָה.
Behold, Hashem, blessed be He, implanted this special power within the tribe of Judah: that he never despairs of himself, no matter what passes over him.
וְהִנֵּה בַּפָּרָשָׁה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת אָמַר "הִנֶּנּוּ עֲבָדִים לַאדֹנִי" וְהָיָה נִרְאֶה שֶׁהִתְחִיל לְיָאֵשׁ אֶת עַצְמוֹ
Now at the end of the previous Torah portion (Miketz), Judah said, "Behold, we are my lord's bondmen," where it seemed as though he were beginning to despair
וְהָיָה נֶחְשַׁב בְּעֵינָיו כִּשְׁגִיאָה מַה שֶּׁהִתְחַיֵּיב אֶת עַצְמוֹ לְאָבִיו בִּשְׁתֵּי עוֹלָמוֹת עַל בִּנְיָמִין,
and to view as a tragic error the fact that he had bound himself to his father under a ban in both worlds for Benjamin's safe return;
וּבְזֹאת הַפָּרָשָׁה הִתְחַזֵּק עַצְמוֹ מְאֹד לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאַף שֶׁעָשִׂיתִי שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ יְכוֹלֶת בְּיַד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהוֹשִׁיעַ לִי,

yet at the opening of this Torah portion he fortified himself immensely before Hashem, blessed be He, declaring in his heart: "Even if I acted improperly in making that rash pledge, nevertheless Hashem, blessed be He, has the power to save me!"
וְזֶה "וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָא", אֵלָיו הַיְינוּ בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף עַד שֶׁהָיָה מוּכְרָח לְהִתְוַדַּע לָהֶם.

And this is the meaning of "Then Judah approached him (eilav)"—"to him" means he penetrated into the very depths of Joseph's heart, until Joseph could no longer restrain himself and was compelled to make himself known to them.
כִּי כָל הַפְּסוּקִים הַלָּלוּ הֵם טַעֲנָה נֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וִיהוּדָא הָיָה סוֹבֵר שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ גּוֹי וּמִתְוַכֵּחַ עִמּוֹ,

For all of these verses in Judah's plea were inwardly directed as a prayerful argument before Hashem, blessed be He, even while outwardly Judah thought he was standing before a gentile ruler and arguing with him;
וְכַאֲשֶׁר שָׁלַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַיְשׁוּעָה אָז רָאוּ שֶׁגַּם לְמַפְרֵעַ לֹא הָיוּ בְּסַכָּנוֹת, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הָיוּ מִתְוַכְּחִים עִם אֲחִיהֶם,

and the moment Hashem, blessed be He, sent them salvation ("I am Joseph!"), they realized that even retroactively they had never been in real danger at all, because in truth they had been arguing with their own loving brother the entire time!
וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד כַּאֲשֶׁר יוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְיִפְדֵּנוּ, אָז יַרְאֶה לָנוּ הַשֵּׁם כִּי לֹא הָיִינוּ בְּגָלוּת מֵעוֹלָם וְלֹא מָשַׁל עָלֵינוּ שׁוּם אוּמָּה רַק הַשֵּׁם לְבַדּוֹ,

And so too in the ultimate future, when Hashem, blessed be He, saves and redeems us, Hashem will show us retroactively that we were never truly under the dominion of exile at all, and that no foreign nation ever ruled over us, but only Hashem alone;
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ הַפָּסוּק (תְּהִלִּים לָמֶד זַיִן, יוֹד) "וְעוֹד מְעַט וְאֵין רָשָׁע וְהִתְבּוֹנַנְתָּ עַל מְקוֹמוֹ וְאֵינֶנּוּ",
and this is the meaning of the verse (Psalms 37:10): "And yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be; yes, you shall contemplate his place, and it shall not be"—

הַיְינוּ בְּעוֹד מְעַט יִתְבַּטֵּל רָשָׁע, "וְהִתְבּוֹנַנְתָּ" הַיְינוּ בְּבִינַת הַלֵּב בְּאִם תִּרְצֶה לְהָבִין עַל מְקוֹמוֹ, "וְאֵינֶנּוּ" הַיְינוּ תִּרְאֶה כִּי לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ מֶמְשָׁלָה עָלֶיךָ.

meaning: in a little while the wicked will be nullified, and when "you contemplate" with the understanding of your heart to examine his former place, "it shall not be"—you will see that even in the past he never possessed any genuine power of dominion over you whatsoever!
h:
The Special Power of Yehudah
Behold, Hashem, blessed be He, implanted this special power within the tribe of Judah: that he never despairs of himself, no matter what passes over him

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 3
p: אֲדֹנִי שָׁאַל אֶת עֲבָדָיו לֵאמֹר הֲיֵשׁ וְכוּלֵי וַנֹּאמֶר וְכוּלֵי וַתֹּאמֶר אֶל עֲבָדֶיךָ הוֹרִידֻהוּ וְכוּלֵי.
My lord asked his servants, saying, "Have you a father, or a brother?" And we said... And you said to your servants, "Bring him down to me," etc.
הִנֵּה אַף כִּי לֹא נִמְצָא בָּזֶה שׁוּם תֵּירוּץ נֶגֶד טַעֲנוֹת הַגְּנֵיבָה שֶׁטָּעַן יוֹסֵף, אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת זֹאת הָיְתָה טַעֲנוֹת יְהוּדָא.

Behold, even though repeating this history seems to offer no legal defense against the charge of stealing the goblet that Joseph leveled against Benjamin, in truth this was the very crux of Judah's argument:
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין הָאָדָם נֶעֱנָשׁ עַל הַחֶסְרוֹן הַנִּמְצָא בוֹ בְּאֵיזֶה עִנְיָן עַד שֶׁיּוֹצִיאוֹ לַפֹּעַל אֶל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
for in heavenly justice a person is never punished for a latent flaw or predisposition lurking within him until he brings it out into actual deed;

וְהִנֵּה אַף אִם בֶּאֱמֶת נִמְצָא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם אֵיזֶה חֶסְרוֹן בְּבִנְיָמִין בְּעִנְיַן גְּנֵיבָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵיתוֹ לֹא הָיָה בָא לִכְלַל מַעֲשֶׂה כָּזֹאת וְרַק קִטְרוּג הַדֶּרֶךְ גָּרַם לוֹ,

now even if, Heaven forbid, some latent susceptibility regarding theft were found in Benjamin, nevertheless had he remained sitting safely at home with his father he would never have come to commit such an act, and it was solely the spiritual peril and temptation of the road and Egypt that caused him to stumble;
וְאִם כֵּן לֹא עָלָיו הָאָשָׁם בַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ עָלָיו, כִּי בִּרְצוֹנוֹ לֹא הָיָה לֵילֵךְ לְדֶרֶךְ מִצְרַיִם,

and if so, the blame for this matter does not rest upon him to be punished for it, since it was never his own will or desire to travel down to Egypt, for you yourself forced us to bring him down against our father's will!
וְזֹאת טָעַן נֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי הֶאֱמִין שֶׁאַף מַה שֶּׁאָמַר יוֹסֵף אֲלֵיהֶם שֶׁיָּבִיאוּ אֶת בִּנְיָמִין לֹא הָיָה בִּלְתִּי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.

And inwardly Judah was directing this very plea before Hashem, blessed be He ("You Yourself compelled us to bring him down into temptation!"), because he believed with complete faith that even the viceroy's demand that they bring Benjamin down was orchestrated solely by the will of Hashem, blessed be He.
h:
Yehudah’s Plea on Behalf of Binyamin
Behold, even though repeating this history seems to offer no legal defense against the charge of stealing the goblet that Joseph leveled against Benjamin, i…

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
p: וַיֹּאמֶר יִשְׂרָאֵל רַב עוֹד יוֹסֵף בְּנִי חָי אֵלְכָה וְאֶרְאֶנּוּ בְּטֶרֶם אָמוּת.
And Israel said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive! I will go and see him before I die."
אִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (בְּרָכוֹת הֵא עַמּוּד אָלֶף) אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי בַּר חָמָא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ,
It is stated in the Gemara (Berakhot 5a): Rabbi Levi bar Chama said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish:
לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם יֵצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרַע, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "רִגְזוּ וְאַל תֶּחֱטָאוּ",
A person should always incite the good inclination against the evil inclination, as it is stated (Psalms 4:5), "Tremble (rigzu), and do not sin";
אִם נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב, וְאִם לָאו יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "אִמְרוּ בִלְבַבְכֶם",
if he conquers it, well and good, and if not, let him engage in Torah study, as it is stated, "commune in your heart";
אִם נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב וְאִם לָאו יִקְרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְעַל מִשְׁכַּבְכֶם",
if he conquers it, well and good, and if not, let him recite the Shema, as it is stated, "upon your bed";
נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב וְאִם לָאו יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְדוֹמּוּ סֶלָה".
if he conquers it, well and good, and if not, let him remind himself of the day of death, as it is stated, "and be silent, Selah."
מַה שֶּׁאָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי בַּר חָמָא לְשׁוֹן לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז, כִּי לְעוֹלָם הַיְינוּ בְּכָל הָעִנְיָנִים שֶׁיַּעַבְרוּ עַל הָאָדָם וְאַף בְּעִנְיְנֵי מַדְרֵגוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת
The reason why Rabbi Levi bar Chama used the word "always" (le'olam) is that in all situations that pass over a person—even in matters of lofty spiritual levels—
צָרִיךְ תָּמִיד לְהַבְחִין וּלְבָרֵר בְּבֵרוּרִין אִם הִיא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹ פֶּן נִמְצָא בָּהּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁמֶץ וְסִיג מִדָּבָר אַחֵר.
one must always test and clarify whether the impulse is purely from Hashem, blessed be He, or whether, Heaven forbid, some trace or dross of self-interest is mixed into it.
וּבִפְרָט כְּשֶׁיָּבֹא לְאָדָם עֵסֶק שִׂמְחָה צָרִיךְ עוֹד יוֹתֵר בֵּירֵר.
And especially when an occasion of great joy comes to a person, it requires even greater scrutiny and clarification (lest it be mere worldly joy).
וְעַל כֵּן נִזְכַּר כָּאן אַרְבָּעָה מַדְרֵגוֹת עֵצוֹת לָאָדָם אֵיךְ לְהַבְחִין וְלָבוֹא עַל עוֹמֶק הָאֱמֶת,
And therefore four successive stages of counsel are given here for how a person can test his emotion and arrive at the depth of truth;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר יֵדַע בְּבֵירֵר כִּי מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם הוּא אָז יָכוֹל לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט עַצְמוֹ וְיֵדַע כִּי הוּא דְּבַר מִצְוָה אוֹ שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה.
and afterward, once it survives all four tests and he knows with clarity that it is from Hashem, he may expand in it freely, knowing that it is a genuine mitzvah or the sacred joy of a mitzvah.
וְהִנֵּה כְּשֶׁיְּאוּנֶּה לָאָדָם אֵיזֶה עֵסֶק מֵעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַצָּרִיךְ בֵּירֵר, עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר בַּגְּמָרָא אַרְבָּעָה בֵּרוּרִים.
Now, when any desire or joy involving this world presents itself to a person and requires testing, the Gemara prescribes four clarifications:
הַבֵּירֵר הָרִאשׁוֹן הוּא לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם יֵצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרַע.
The first test is: "A person should always incite the good inclination against the evil inclination"—

הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּפְסִיק אֶת חֶמְדָּתוֹ בִּנְתִינָתוֹ אֶל לִבּוֹ שֶׁזֹּאת הַחֶמְדָּה לֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, כִּי יְמֵי שְׁנוֹתֵינוּ בָהֶם שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה וְלָמָּה לִי טוֹבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ קַיֶּימֶת לָעַד.

meaning that he should interrupt his desire by taking to heart that this worldly pleasure will not remain his forever, for "the days of our years are seventy years" (Psalms 90:10), and "what use to me is a fleeting pleasure that does not endure forever?"
נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב וְאִם לָאו יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה.
"If he conquers it (and the desire vanishes, proving it was merely temporal), well and good; and if not, let him engage in Torah":

כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׂם בְּדַעְתּוֹ כִּי לֹא לָעַד יִהְיֶה לוֹ זֹאת הַחֶמְדָּה וְעוֹד יִשְׁתּוֹקֵק לָהּ, נִרְאֶה קְצָת שֶׁהוּא חֶמְדָּה קַיֶּימֶת, אַךְ עוֹד צָרִיךְ לְבָרֵר בֵּירֵר הַשֵּׁנִי, וְהוּא שֶׁיַּעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה

for if, even after reflecting on mortality, the yearning still persists in his heart, this is a preliminary sign that it may be an eternal, holy desire; yet he must still subject it to the second test, which is to immerse himself in Torah study;

כִּי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה הֵם עֵצָה לָאָדָם לְהִנָּצֵל מֵחֶמְדָּה, אַף בְּעִידָּנָא דְּיֵצֶר הָרַע דְּלֵית מַאן דְּמִדְּכִיר לְיֵצֶר טוֹב (נְדָרִים לָמֶד בֵּית עַמּוּד בֵּית), עַל זֶה בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין,

for words of Torah are the ultimate counsel to save a person from base craving—even at the hour when the evil inclination rages and no one remembers the good inclination (Nedarim 32b), for which the Holy One, blessed be He, created the Torah as an antidote and "spice" (Kiddushin 30b);

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הָאָדָם הַמְּשׁוּקָּע בְּחֵשֶׁק וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִנָּצֵל מִמֶּנּוּ, אָז אֵין לוֹ עֵצָה שֶׁיִּזְכּוֹר כִּי הוּא דָּבָר אָסוּר, כִּי אֵין כֹּחַ בְּהָאִיסּוּר כָּל כָּךְ לְהַפְרִישׁ אֶת הָאָדָם מֵרָע בְּעִידָּנָא דְּיֵצֶר הָרַע,

because in truth, when a person is plunged in burning desire and feels unable to extricate himself from it, merely reminding himself that the thing is forbidden will not avail him, for a bare prohibition lacks the power to pull a person away from evil at the height of passion;
אַךְ אָז הָעֵצָה הַיְּעוּצָה לָאָדָם שֶׁיִּזְכּוֹר, כִּי יוּכַל לִמְצֹא זֶה הַטּוֹבָה עַצְמָהּ בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וְרַק שֶׁיְּהֵא בִּקְדוּשָּׁה,
rather, the effective counsel then is for the person to remember and taste that he can find that very same sweetness and delight within words of Torah in complete holiness!
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר עַל פָּסוּק "הַיָּם רָאָה וַיָּנוֹס", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם כִּי רָאָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַהֲפוֹךְ אֶת הַצּוּר לַאֲגַם מַיִם וְחַלָּמִישׁ לְמַעְיְנוֹ מַיִם,

And this is as was explained on the verse "The sea saw and fled" (Psalms 114:3)—why did the sea flee? Because it saw at the end of the psalm that Hashem, blessed be He, "turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a fountain of waters" (Psalms 114:8);
וּמֵהַצּוֹרֶךְ לִכְתּוֹב לְהֵיפֶךְ כִּי רָאָה גְּבוּרוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי יָכוֹל לְהַחֲרִיב וּלְיַבֵּשׁ אֶת הַיָּם,
now seemingly, Scripture should have written the reverse—that the sea fled because it saw the might of Hashem, blessed be He, Who can dry up and destroy the sea!
אַךְ כִּי יָם מְרַמֵּז עַל תַּאֲוָה וּבְעֵת שֶׁהַתַּאֲוָה מִתְגַּבֶּרֶת אֵין עֵצָה כְּנֶגְדָּהּ רַק לְהַרְאוֹת כִּי נִמְצָא כָּזֹאת בִּקְדוּשָּׁה וְאָז תִּפָּסֵק,

However, the "sea" alludes to raging worldly desire, and when desire surges, there is no counsel against it except to show the soul that the very same pleasure ("fountains of water") can be drawn from the Rock of Holiness (Torah), and then the unholy craving automatically subsides!
[וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב (דְּבָרִים חֵית, טֵית וָאו) "הַמּוֹצִיא לְךָ מַיִם מִצּוּר הַחַלָּמִישׁ", [
And this is what is written (Deuteronomy 8:15), "Who brought forth water for you out of the rock of flint"—
הַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל הַתַּעֲנוּגִים נִמְצָאִים בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וְהֵמָּה מְיוּפִּים בְּכָל מִינֵי יוֹפִי וּכְשֶׁיִּזְכּוֹר הָאָדָם זֹאת, אֲזַי יִשְׁקוֹט הַיָּם מִזַּעְפּוֹ
meaning that all delights are found within words of Torah, adorned with every kind of beauty, and when a person remembers this, the stormy sea of lust quiets from its raging—

כְּמוֹ אִם יָרוּץ אָדָם בְּבֶהָלָה לְמַלֹּאוֹת רַעֲבוֹנוֹ וַחֲבֵירוֹ יוֹכִיחוֹ עַל מְהִירוּת בֶּהָלָתוֹ וְיִרְצֶה לַעֲצוֹר אוֹתוֹ לִבְלִי יְמַהֵר לָרוּץ כָּל כָּךְ, בֶּטַח לֹא יִשְׁמַע לוֹ, כִּי הוּא מְבוֹהָל מֵחֲמַת רַעֲבוֹנוֹ

just as if a starving man is running franticly to satisfy his hunger and his friend rebukes him for his frantic haste and tries to restrain him from running so fast, he will surely not listen to him because he is driven by hunger;
אֲבָל אִם חֲבֵירוֹ יֹאמַר לוֹ לָמָּה לְךָ לָרוּץ שֵׁב בְּבֵיתְךָ וְשָׁם יֵשׁ כָּל מִשְׁאֲלוֹתֶיךָ בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, בֶּטַח יִשְׁמַע לוֹ. תַּשְׁלוּם.]

whereas if his friend tells him, "Why run out there? Sit in your own home, where a royal banquet fulfilling all your desires is already spread before you in far greater abundance!"—he will surely listen to him and stop running. End of addendum.
] וְזֶהוּ הָעֵצָה יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה.
And this is the counsel: "let him engage in Torah."
נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב וְאִם לָאו יִקְרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע,
"If he conquers it, well and good; and if not, let him recite the Shema":
כִּי בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה נִמְצָא הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת וְיוּכַל הָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה לְהַרְהִיב עוֹז בְּנַפְשׁוֹ וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה לֹא יוּכַל לָבוֹא לִידֵי בֵּירֵר הָאֲמִיתִּי,

for within the study of Torah there is an element of spiritual self-elevation and vigor, so that through Torah study a person might feel emboldened in his soul and still fail to arrive at complete, humble clarity regarding his desire;

וְלָזֶה הָעֵצָה יִקְרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע כִּי עִנְיַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע הוּא כַּמְּבוֹאָר בַּגְּמָרָא (תַּעֲנִית לָמֶד אָלֶף עַמּוּד אָלֶף) עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת מָחוֹל לַצַּדִּיקִים,

therefore the third test is to recite the Shema ("Hashem is One"), for the essence of the Shema corresponds to what is explained in the Gemara (Ta'anit 31a), that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance (machol) for the righteous—

הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַכֹּל יִרְאוּ כִּי כָּל דָּבָר בְּיַד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵין לְאֶחָד שׁוּם יִתְרוֹן וְהִתְנַשְּׂאוּת עַל חֲבֵירוֹ, כִּי מָחוֹל הַיְינוּ דָּבָר עָגוֹל שֶׁאֵין לוֹ סוֹף וְעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז עִנְיַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.

meaning that all will see that everything is equally in the hand of Hashem, blessed be He, and no individual has any superiority or self-exaltation over his fellow, just like a circle which has no head or end; and the unification of the Shema alludes to this complete nullification of self.
נְצָחוֹ מוּטָב וְאִם לָאו יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה.
"If he conquers it, well and good; and if not, let him remind himself of the day of death":
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר בְּמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ כְּאִילּוּ עַכְשָׁיו הוּא יוֹם הַמִּיתָה, וְזֶה הוּא הַחִילּוּק שֶׁל יַרְגִּיז שֶׁגַּם כֵּן יִתְפָּרֵשׁ כְּעִנְיָן זֶה,

meaning that he should vividly picture in his mind as if right now were the actual moment of his death—and this is how the fourth stage differs from the first stage ("incite"), which merely reflected on the fact that life eventually ends after seventy years—
אַךְ יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר בְּמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ כְּאִלּוּ עַתָּה זְמַן הַמִּיתָה וְאִם כֵּן אֵין לְהַחֶמְדָּה וְהַשִּׂמְחָה שׁוּם מָקוֹם,
for here he pictures in his thought as though he were dying at this very instant, in which case no temporal desire or worldly joy can possibly have any place!
וּבְאִם אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר עוֹד בְּלִבּוֹ הַחֶמְדָּה אוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז רְאָיָה כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הִיא וְתִתְקַיֵּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד,

And if, after passing through all four of these crucible-tests, the yearning or the joy still remains undiminished in his heart, that is absolute proof that it comes from Hashem and will endure for all eternity!

וְכֵן הוּא הָעִנְיָן בְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ בְּעֵת שֶׁשָּׁמַע הַבְּשׂוֹרָה כִּי עוֹד יוֹסֵף חַי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַתְּחִי רוּחַ יַעֲקֹב", וְהָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ פֶּן הַשִּׂמְחָה הַזֹּאת הִיא רַק שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל כֵּן בָּחַן וְצֵירֵף אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּאֵלּוּ הַבֵּרוּרִים,

And this was the exact process enacted by our father Jacob when he heard the tidings that Joseph was still alive: when it is stated, "and the spirit of Jacob their father revived," he feared for his soul lest this overwhelming joy be merely the natural, worldly joy of a father reunited with his son; therefore he tested and refined himself through all four of these clarifications:
הַבֵּירֵר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁאָמַר "אֵלְכָה וְאֶרְאֶנּוּ בְּטֶרֶם אָמוּת", הוּא נֶגֶד לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר,

the first test was when he said, "I will go and see him before I die" (reminding himself that his life in this world was nearing its end), corresponding to "let a person always incite," as explained above;

וְהַשֵּׁנִי "וַיִּזְבַּח זְבָחִים לֵאלֹקֵי אָבִיו יִצְחָק", זֶה נֶגֶד יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין בְּכָל יוֹם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לַעֲסוֹק בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה, כִּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בִּנְתִינַת הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא גְּבוּרָה כָּךְ שָׁמַע מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה (מְגִילָּה לָמֶד אָלֶף עַמּוּד בֵּית) כַּיָּדוּעַ לַמֵּבִין,

and the second test was "and he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac," which corresponds to "let him engage in Torah"—just as we bless every day "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to engage in words of Torah"—for at the Giving of the Torah the Holy One, blessed be He, is called Gevurah (the attribute of Isaac), as in "Thus Moses heard from the mouth of the Gevurah" (Megillah 31b), as is known to the insightful;
וְשָׁם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי אַעַלְךָ גַם עָלֹה" אֲשֶׁר הוּא נֶגֶד הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ", רַק שָׁם הוּא לֶעָבָר וְהָכָא הוּא לֶעָתִיד,

and there in Beersheba God spoke to him the utterance, "I (Anokhi) will go down with you into Egypt, and I will also surely bring you up" (Genesis 46:4), which directly parallels the opening of the Ten Commandments at Sinai, "I (Anokhi) am Hashem your God Who brought you out of the land of Egypt," except that at Sinai it is in the past tense and here it is in the future tense;

וְגַם מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו" וּפֵירְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּגַּשׁ יוֹד אָלֶף) לְתַקֵּן לוֹ בֵּית תַּלְמוּד הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיָן הַלָּזֶה,

and furthermore, what is stated afterward, "And he sent Judah before him to Joseph, to direct before him (lehorot lefanav) unto Goshen," which our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Midrash Tanchuma, Vayigash 11; Bereishit Rabbah 95:3) as "to establish a house of Torah study for him," was also part of this second stage of engaging in Torah;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ בֵּירֵר בַּבֵּירֵר הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַיֵּבְךְּ עַל צַוָּארָיו עוֹד וְדָרְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מְלַמֵּד שֶׁקָּרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע,

and afterward, at the moment of meeting Joseph, he tested his joy with the third clarification: "and he wept on his neck a good while," while Jacob himself did not kiss him—which our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Rashi on Genesis 46:29) as teaching that Jacob was reciting the Shema!
וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר לְיוֹסֵף "אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם" הוּא נֶגֶד עֵצָה הָרְבִיעִית יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה,

And immediately afterward he said to Joseph, "Now let me die (amutah hapa'am), since I have seen your face," which corresponds to the fourth counsel: "let him remind himself of the day of death" (picturing death at that very moment);
וּכְשֶׁרָאָה יַעֲקֹב כִּי אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר לוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז הֵבִין כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הוּא וְהוּא שִׂמְחָה אֲמִיתִּית וְקַיָּים לָעַד.

and when Jacob saw that after all four of these tests the joy still remained radiant within him ("that you are yet alive"), he knew with certainty that this joy was from Hashem and was a true, holy joy that would endure forever.
h:
Yaakov Learns That Yosef Is Alive
Rabbi Levi bar Chama said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 5
p: וַיִּזְבַּח זְבָחִים לֵאלֹקֵי אָבִיו יִצְחָק.
And he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.

הָעִנְיָן שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשֵׁם אֱלֹקֵי יִצְחָק, כִּי יַעֲקֹב הִתְפַּלֵּל אֶל מַאֲמָר הַזֶּה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לְיִצְחָק אָבִינוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית כָּף וָאו, גִּימֶל) "גּוּר בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת",

Another reason why Hashem, blessed be He, is specifically called here "the God of his father Isaac" is because Jacob was praying concerning the divine command that had been spoken to our father Isaac during the famine (Genesis 26:2–3): "Go not down into Egypt... sojourn in this land";
וְהָיָה מִתְיָרֵא פֶּן גַּם לוֹ אָסוּר לָצֵאת, לָכֵן הִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַד שֶׁהֵאִיר עֵינָיו כִּי לוֹ מוּתָּר לָצֵאת.

and Jacob was afraid lest he too be forbidden to leave the Land of Israel for Egypt, and therefore he offered sacrifices and prayed to Hashem, blessed be He, until He illuminated his eyes ("Fear not to go down into Egypt"), assuring him that he was permitted to depart.

Offerings to the God of Yitzchak

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 6
p: וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו.
And he sent Judah before him.
אִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּגַּשׁ וָאו) הֱוֵי זְהִירִין בַּמִּצְוֹת שֶׁהֵם שְׁלוּחֵי וְכוּלֵי.
It is stated in the Midrash (cf. Tanchuma Vayigash 6): Be heedful of the mitzvot, for they are emissaries, etc.
כִּי מַדְרֵגוֹת יוֹסֵף הוּא קִיּוּם הַמִּצְוֹת וּמַדְרֵגוֹת יְהוּדָא הוּא בִּרְכוֹת הַמִּצְוֹת,

For the spiritual rung of Joseph is the practical fulfillment of the mitzvot, whereas the spiritual rung of Judah (whose name means thanksgiving and praise) is the recitation of the blessings over the mitzvot (Birkhot HaMitzvot);
וְכָל הַמִּצְוֹת מְבָרֵךְ עֲלֵיהֶם עוֹבֵר לַעֲשִׂיָּיתָן, וְזֶה הוּא הָעִנְיָן "וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו".

and the halakhic rule regarding all mitzvot is that one recites the blessing over them immediately prior to their performance (over la'asiyatan, Pesachim 7b)—and this is the inner meaning of "And he sent Judah (the blessing) before him (ahead of meeting Joseph, the mitzvah)."
h:
Sending Yehudah Ahead to Goshen
Be heedful of the mitzvot, for they are emissaries, etc

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 7
p: וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בְּאֶרֶץ גּוֹשֶׁן.
And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen.

לֶהֱיוֹת כִּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ הָיָה מִתְיָרֵא לֵילֵךְ לְחוּץ לָאָרֶץ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (כְּתוּבּוֹת קוּף יוֹד עַמּוּד בֵּית) כָּל הַדָּר בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל דּוֹמֶה כְּמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אֱלֹקִים וְכוּלֵי,

Because our father Jacob was afraid to go down outside the Land of Israel—as is stated in the Gemara (Ketubot 110b), "Whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God, and whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God"—
וְאָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי בְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה שָׁם הוּא קָדוֹשׁ בִּקְדוּשַּׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל,
Hashem, blessed be He, assured him that "wherever you dwell becomes sanctified with the holiness of the Land of Israel";

וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בְּאֶרֶץ גּוֹשֶׁן, הַיְינוּ שֶׁאַף בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם הָיָה קָרוֹב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהָיָה מָקוֹם מְקוּדָּשׁ, כִּי גּוֹשֶׁן הִיא לְשׁוֹן הִתְקָרְבוּת.

and this is the meaning of "And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen": namely, that even in the land of Egypt he remained close and bound to Hashem, blessed be He, in a sanctified place, for "Goshen" (גּוֹשֶׁן) is an expression of drawing near (הִתְקָרְבוּת / נְגִישָׁה, as in וַיִּגַּשׁ).

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 1
p: וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב.
And Jacob lived.
אִיתָא בְּמַסֶּכֶת אָבוֹת [פֶּרֶק גִּימֶל, מִשְׁנָה יוֹד זַיִן] אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת.
It is stated in Tractate Avot (3:17): "If there is no understanding (binah), there is no knowledge (da'at); if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding."

בִּינָה הַיְינוּ הַכְּלָלִים שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה, הַיְינוּ טַעֲמֵי הַדְּבָרִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּמְצָא כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים זֶה הַכְּלָל וְעַל יְדֵי הַכְּלָל יִוָּדַע לָאָדָם כַּמָּה פְּרָטִים, וְדַעַת הַיְינוּ הַפְּרָטִים.

"Understanding" (Binah) refers to the overarching principles (kelalim) of the words of Torah—namely, the underlying reasons of matters, as we often find in the Mishnah "This is the general principle (zeh hakelal)," through which a person comes to know numerous specific laws—whereas "Knowledge" (Da'at) refers to the specific, practical details (peratim).
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת הַיְינוּ אִם אֵין הָאָדָם יוֹדֵעַ הַכְּלָל שֶׁהוּא טַעַם הַדָּבָר אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לָדַעַת הַפְּרָט, כִּי מִפְּרָט אֶחָד לֹא יִוָּדַע פְּרָט הַשֵּׁנִי.

And this is the meaning of "If there is no binah, there is no da'at": if a person does not grasp the general principle, which is the underlying rationale of the matter, he cannot truly know the specifics, because from one isolated detail alone he will not know how to adjudicate a second detail.
וְכֵן לְהֵפֶךְ, אִם אֵין דַּעַת אֵין בִּינָה הַיְינוּ אִם תִּמְצָא לֵאמֹר אֵדַע הַכְּלָל וְלֹא אֶצְטָרֵךְ לִלְמוֹד הַפְּרָט,
And conversely, "if there is no da'at, there is no binah": if you should think to say, "I will suffice with knowing the general principle and will not need to study the specific details,"
עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ אִם אֵין דַּעַת הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ מְסוּדָּרִים אֶצְלְךָ הַפְּרָטִים, לֹא תֵּדַע שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַכְּלָל לַאֲמִיתּוֹ אֵיךְ יוּכַל לְהִסְתַּעֵף.

concerning this they taught that "if there is no da'at"—meaning if the practical details are not clearly ordered before you—you do not truly grasp the root of the general principle and how it branches out into actuality!
וְזֶהוּ "וַיְחִי" הַיְינוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַחַיִּים וְהוּא הַכְּלָל שֶׁל כָּל דָּבָר, וְיַעֲקֹב הַיְינוּ דַּעַת הוּא הַפְּרָט,

And this is the inner meaning of "And Jacob lived (Vayechi Yaakov)": "Vayechi" signifies the supernal Root of Life (Binah), which is the overarching principle of everything, while "Yaakov" signifies Da'at, which is the specific detail—
כִּי יַעֲקֹב מְכוּנֶּה נֶגֶד זְעֵיר אַנְפִּין הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁגִּיחַ עַל כָּל פְּרָט עַל כָּל דְּבָרִים הַנִּצְרָכִים לוֹ, אֲפִילּוּ קָטָן שֶׁבַּקְּטַנִּים.

for in Kabbalah Jacob corresponds to Ze'ir Anpin (linked with Da'at), signifying that Hashem, blessed be He, exercises individual providence over every single detail and everything required for it, down to the smallest of the small.
h:
Vayechi: Yaakov’s True Life
17): "If there is no understanding (binah), there is no knowledge (da'at); if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 2
p: שִׂכֵּל אֶת יָדָיו.
He guided his hands wittingly (crossing his arms).
לֶהֱיוֹת כִּי יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ הָיָה מַדְרֵגָתוֹ מִדּוֹת הַגְּבוּרָה, וְלָכֵן רָצָה לְבָרֵךְ אֶת עֵשָׂו,
Since the spiritual rung of our father Isaac was the attribute of Gevurah (strict justice and law), he originally intended to bless Esau:
כִּי מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה מוֹרָה עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה (מְגִילָּה לָמֶד אָלֶף עַמּוּד בֵּית) כָּךְ שָׁמַע מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה וְלָכֵן אָמַר יִקּוֹב הַדִּין אֶת הָהָר,

for the attribute of Gevurah indicates the formal law of the Torah—as in "Thus Moses heard from the mouth of the Gevurah" (Megillah 31b)—and therefore Isaac's approach was "Let the strict law pierce the mountain" (Sanhedrin 6b),
וּלְכָךְ לֹא הָיָה בְּכֹחוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת נֶגֶד הַמִּשְׁפָּט וְרָצָה לְבָרֵךְ אֶת עֵשָׂו בְּיַעַן כִּי הָיָה בְּכוֹר.
and consequently he felt unable on his own initiative to act contrary to the formal rule of primogeniture, and sought to bless Esau because he was the firstborn.
אַךְ כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ סוֹמֵךְ יָדַיִם טְהוֹרוֹת כִּי הַיָּדַיִם הֵם עַנְפֵי הַלֵּב, וְלִבּוֹ הָיָה טָהוֹר וּמְזֻכָּךְ וְסִיבֵּב הַדָּבָר שֶׁיְּבָרֵךְ אֶת יַעֲקֹב בְּלֹא דַּעְתּוֹ,

However, because Hashem, blessed be He, supports pure hands—for the hands are the branches of the heart, and Isaac's heart was utterly pure and refined—Hashem orchestrated events so that Isaac's hands blessed Jacob without his conscious awareness,
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר (תְּהִלִּים טֵית זַיִן, הֵא) "אַתָּה תּוֹמִיךְ גּוֹרָלִי",
and concerning this it is stated (Psalms 16:5): "You guide my lot";
אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ הָיָה מִסְתַּכֵּל תָּמִיד אֶל הַבִּינָה וְלִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
whereas our father Jacob gazed constantly into the supernal Binah (the inner root of truth beyond formal precedence) and the true will of Hashem, blessed be He,
וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר "יָדַעְתִּי בְנִי יָדַעְתִּי" "שִׂכֵּל אֶת יָדָיו", "וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת אֶפְרַיִם לִפְנֵי מְנַשֶּׁה".

and therefore regarding Jacob it is stated with full conscious awareness: "I know, my son, I know," and "he guided his hands wittingly (sikeil et yadav—with deliberate wisdom), for Manasseh was the firstborn," and "he set Ephraim before Manasseh."
h:
Yaakov Crosses His Hands over Ephraim and Menashe
Since the spiritual rung of our father Isaac was the attribute of Gevurah (strict justice and law), he originally intended to bless Esau

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 3
p: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאֱלֹקִים אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ אֲבוֹתַי לְפָנָיו הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי.
And he blessed Joseph, and said: "The God before Whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God Who has been my shepherd all my life long unto this day."
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ הָיָה מַקְטִין עַצְמוֹ נֶגֶד אֲבוֹתָיו אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק,
That is, our father Jacob was humbling himself in comparison to his fathers Abraham and Isaac:
וְאָמַר כִּי לָהֶם הָיָה חָכְמָה וּבִינָה גְּדוֹלָה מְאֹד עַד כִּי הִרְחִיבוּ אֶת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעַצְמָם,
for he said that they possessed such vast wisdom and understanding that they were able to expand and deduce the will of Hashem, blessed be He, on their own initiative,

וְאַף אִם פָּתַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פֶּתַח קָטָן, הָיוּ מַרְחִיבִים וּמִתְפַּשְּׁטִים אוֹתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתָם כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן בּוֹרְאָם, וְהֵבִינוּ אַף בְּדָבָר שֶׁלֹּא הֵאִיר לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְפֹרָשׁ,

so that even when Hashem, blessed be He, opened only a small aperture of illumination for them, they would broaden and expand it through their wisdom in order to fulfill the will of their Creator, understanding what to do even in matters that Hashem, blessed be He, had not explicitly illuminated for them—
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ" הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיוּ הוֹלְכִים בְּכֹחָם.
and this is the meaning of "before Whom my fathers walked (hithalkhu)," in the reflexive form, indicating that they walked forward by their own spiritual power.

אֲבָל אֲנִי, "הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה", הַיְינוּ בְּכָל פְּרָט מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה, אֲנִי צָרִיךְ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָאִיר עֵינַי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,

"As for me, however," said Jacob, "'the God Who shepherds me from my inception unto this day'—meaning that in every single detailed action that I perform, I need Hashem, blessed be He, to guide me like a shepherd and illuminate my eyes as to what His will, blessed be He, is;
וְאַף בְּזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁרָאִיתִי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ, אִם רְצוֹנוֹ לְשַׁנּוֹתָהּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ אֲנִי לִרְאוֹת גַּם בַּפַּעַם הַשֵּׁנִית אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,

and even regarding an action where I already saw what His will was yesterday, since His will might change according to the hour, I still need to look to Him afresh the second time to see what His will, blessed be He, is right now!"
וּבֶאֱמֶת בְּזֶה הָעִנְיָן הָיָה יַעֲקֹב הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּאָבוֹת כִּי זֹאת הִיא מַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַנְהִיג אֶת הָאָדָם תָּמִיד,

And while Jacob said this out of humility, in truth it was precisely in this quality that Jacob was the greatest of the Patriarchs! For it is the highest spiritual rung of all when Hashem, blessed be He, Himself continuously guides a person at every step;
וְזֹאת הָיְתָה תְּפִלַּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (תְּהִלִּים כָּף גִּימֶל, אָלֶף) "הַשֵּׁם רוֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר",
and this was the prayer of King David, peace be upon him (Psalms 23:1): "Hashem is my shepherd; I shall not lack (lo echsar)"—
הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְסִיר הַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עָלַי וְרַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רוֹעֶה אוֹתִי תָּמִיד וְגַם אֲנִי אַכִּיר תָּמִיד שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא רוֹעִי,
meaning: "May I never cause Hashem's direct providence over me to be lacking, rather may He shepherd me constantly, and may I too constantly recognize that Hashem, blessed be He, is my Shepherd!"
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּטוּבוֹ מַנְהִיג כָּל דָּבָר, אַךְ שֶׁהָאָדָם מַחְזִיר פָּנָיו וְאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְצַפּוֹת וּלְהִתְפַּלֵּל,
For Hashem, blessed be He, in His goodness guides everything, except that man turns his face away and relies on himself rather than waiting and praying to Him;
וּבְעֵת שֶׁהָאָדָם יִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה שְׁלֵימָה אָז תֵּיכֶף יֵעָנֶה, וְיִרְאֶה כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הָרוֹעֶה וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "לֹא אֶחְסָר" הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְזִיר פָּנַי מִמֶּנּוּ.

whereas whenever a person offers a complete prayer from the heart, he is immediately answered and sees tangibly that Hashem, blessed be He, is his Shepherd—and this is the meaning of "I shall not lack (lo echsar)," namely, may I never turn my face away from depending upon Him.
h:
Yaakov’s Blessing to Yosef
That is, our father Jacob was humbling himself in comparison to his fathers Abraham and Isaac

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 4
p: וַיִּקְרָא יַעֲקֹב אֶל בָּנָיו.
And Jacob called unto his sons.
בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (תַּנְחוּמָא וַיְחִי חֵית) "אֶקְרָא לֵאלֹקִים עֶלְיוֹן לָאֵל גּוֹמֵר עָלָי".
In the Midrash (Tanchuma, Vayechi 8; Bereishit Rabbah 98:2) this verse is linked with: "I will call (ekra) unto God Most High, unto God Who completes (gomer) for me" (Psalms 57:3).

הָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר רָצָה יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לְבָרֵךְ אֶת בָּנָיו, הָיָה מְסֻפָּק אִם צָרִיךְ לְבָרֵךְ אוֹתָם מֵחֲמַת שֶׁצִּעֲרוּהוּ בִּמְכִירַת יוֹסֵף וְכָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ נוֹקֵם וְנוֹטֵר וְכוּלֵי (יוֹמָא כָּף בֵּית עַמּוּד בֵּית)

The inner meaning of this is that when our father Jacob wished to bless his sons before his passing, he was in doubt whether he was permitted to bless the first three brothers, since they had caused him immense anguish in the sale of Joseph (and in the incidents of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi), and the Gemara states (Yoma 22b) that "any Torah scholar who does not avenge and bear a grudge like a serpent is not a true Torah scholar" (where the honor of Heaven and Torah is at stake);
לָכֵן נֶאֱמַר "וַיִּקְרָא" לְשׁוֹן צְעָקָה וְקִוּוּי בַּלֵּב שֶׁהָיָה תּוֹלֶה עֵינָיו וְלִבּוֹ לַמָּרוֹם וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר יָשִׂים הַשֵּׁם בְּפִיו אוֹתוֹ יֹאמַר,

therefore it is stated "And Jacob called (vayikra)"—an expression of crying out and hoping in his heart to God ("I will call unto God Most High"), lifting his eyes and heart to Heaven so that whatever Hashem placed in his mouth, that alone he would speak;
וְזֶה כַּוָּונַת הַמִּדְרָשׁ שֶׁהִזְכִּיר זֶה הַפָּסוּק שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ מֵהַשֵּׁם שֶׁיִּגְמוֹר בַּעֲדוֹ.
and this is the intention of the Midrash in citing the verse "unto God Who completes for me"—that Jacob prayed to Hashem to decide and complete the blessings through his mouth.
וְלֹא נֶאֱמַר תְּחִילָּה לְשׁוֹן בְּרָכָה כִּי עוֹד לֹא הָיָה מְבוֹרָר אֶצְלוֹ מַה יֹּאמַר לָהֶם,
And that is why no mention of "blessing" is written at the beginning of Jacob's address, because it was not yet clarified in his mind whether his words would emerge as rebuke or blessing;
אֲבָל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִתְחִיל תֵּיכֶף "וְזֹאת הַבְּרָכָה" כִּי מִילַּת "וְזֹאת" מוֹרָה עַל זֶה שֶׁהָיוּ כָּל הַדְּבָרִים מְבוֹרָרִים אֶצְלוֹ מִיָּד כְּשֶׁהִתְחִיל לְדַבֵּר,

whereas Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, began immediately with the words "And this is the blessing (Vezot haberakhah)" (Deuteronomy 33:1), for the word "this (zot)" indicates that all the blessings were already completely clear before him as soon as he began to speak;
וּבְיַעֲקֹב לֹא נֶאֱמַר "וְזֹאת" רַק אַחַר כָּל הַבְּרָכוֹת שֶׁרַק אָז אַחַר כָּל הַדְּבָרִים הָיוּ אֶצְלוֹ מְבוֹרָרִים שֶׁכָּל בִּרְכוֹתָיו הֵמָּה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא מִקּוֹדֶם.

whereas regarding Jacob, the phrase "And this (Vezot)" is stated only at the very end, after all the blessings ("And this is what their father spoke to them, and blessed them," Genesis 49:28), because only then, after all the words had been spoken, did it become fully clear to him that all his words were indeed blessings from Hashem, blessed be He, and not beforehand.
וְהִנֵּה תְּחִילָּה נָתַן הַשֵּׁם דְּבָרִים שֶׁל קִנְטוּר בְּפִיו לְקַנְטֵר הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה שְׁבָטִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, כִּי תַּלְמִיד חָכָם צָרִיךְ לִנְקוֹם וְלִנְטוֹר

And behold, initially Hashem placed words of rebuke in his mouth to chastise the first three tribes (Reuben, Simeon, and Levi), fulfilling the principle that a Torah scholar must rebuke and hold accountable;
וּכְשֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְשֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָא אָז הֶרְאָהוּ הַשֵּׁם מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לְהַעֲבִיר עַל מִדּוֹתָיו,
yet when he reached the fourth son, Judah, Hashem showed him from Heaven to waive his retributive measure and overflow with pure blessing!

כִּי בְּאוֹתִיּוֹת יְהוּדָא נִמְצָא שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהַדָּלֶ"ת שֶׁבִּשְׁמוֹ מְרַמֵּז עַל פָּסוּק (יְשַׁעְיָה סָמֶךְ וָאו, בֵּית) "וְאֶל זֶה אַבִּיט אֶל עָנִי וּנְכֵה רוּחַ וְחָרֵד עַל דְּבָרִי".

For within the letters of the name "Yehudah" (יְהוּדָה) is spelled the four-letter Name of Havayah (י-ה-ו-ה, the Name of pure Mercy), blessed be He, together with the letter Dalet (ד, meaning "poor/humble"), which alludes to the verse (Isaiah 66:2), "But to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembles at My word"—
הַיְינוּ שֶׁמֵּבִין כִּי אֵין לוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ כְּלוּם כִּדְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (זוֹהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית רֵישׁ מֵם דָּלֶת עַמּוּד בֵּית) דָּלֶ"ת לָקֵיט,
meaning one who recognizes that he possesses nothing at all of his own, just as is stated in the Zohar (Bereishit 244b) that the poor letter Dalet gathers and receives everything from Above;
עַל כֵּן לֹא הָיָה בָּזֶה מָקוֹם לָחוּל שׁוּם כַּעַס וָרוֹגֶז כְּלָל,
therefore, against such humble self-nullification there was no place for any anger or harsh judgment to take hold at all!
וְכַאֲשֶׁר נִפְתַּח בִּיהוּדָא מִדּוֹת הָרַחֲמִים נִתְגַּבֵּר גַּם עַל שְׁאָר הַשְּׁבָטִים וְנִכְלְלוּ כֻּלָּן בַּבְּרָכָה.

And once the attribute of Mercy was unlocked through Judah, it prevailed over all the remaining tribes—and retroactively over the first three as well—so that all twelve were encompassed in blessing ("each according to his blessing he blessed them").
h:
Yaakov Gathers His Sons to Reveal the End

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 5
p: וּבְדַם עֲנָבִים סוּתֹה.
He washes his garments in wine, and his robe (sutoh) in the blood of grapes.
סוּתֹה הַיְינוּ לְשׁוֹן הֲסָתָה כִּי הַהֲסָתָה שֶׁל שׁוֹרֶשׁ יְהוּדָא הִיא אַחֲרֵי הַחֵטְא וּמִכְשׁוֹל שֶׁאֵירַע לוֹ יִתְעוֹרֵר עוֹז בְּנַפְשׁוֹ,

The word "sutoh" is an expression of incitement and enticement (hasatah, cf. Rashi): for the special holy incitement rooted in Judah is that even after a sin and stumbling have befallen him, a fierce fortitude awakens in his soul to declare:
אֵין זֹאת רַק שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִרְצֶה לְהוֹשִׁיעֵנִי בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת,
"This stumbling could only have happened because Hashem, blessed be He, desires to bring me to an even greater elevation and salvation through repentance!"
כִּי עֲנָבִים הַיְינוּ טָעוּת וְשִׁכְחָה, וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ אָמַר (דְּבָרִים לָמֶד בֵּית, יוֹד דָּלֶת) "וְדַם עֵנָב תִּשְׁתֶּה חָמֶר",

For intoxicating "grapes" (anavim) symbolize error and spiritual forgetfulness, and Moses our teacher said in the singular (Deuteronomy 32:14), "and of the blood of the grape (einav) you drank foaming wine (chamer)"—
חָמֶר מוֹרֶה עַל "עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה אֱלֹקִים זוּלָתְךָ" כִּי אֵין מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת מַכִּירִין בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲרָמִי (שַׁבָּת יוֹד בֵּית עַמּוּד בֵּית).

where the Aramaic word chamer (referring to the "wine stored in its grapes since the six days of Creation") indicates the hidden reward of the penitent concerning which it is said, "No eye has seen it, O God, beside You" (Isaiah 64:3; Berakhot 34b), for the ministering angels do not understand the Aramaic tongue (Shabbat 12b) and cannot fathom the mystery of repentance.

רַק מֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו וְיַעֲקֹב מִלְּבַר, כִּי אֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב נֶאֱמַר עֲנָבִים הַיְינוּ שְׁנֵי טָעוּתִים יְבָרֵר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל שֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָא הַיְינוּ יִצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת וְיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וּבֵירֵר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא נָקִי בִּשְׁתֵּיהֶן,

Now why did Jacob say "blood of grapes (anavim)" in the plural, whereas Moses said "blood of the grape (einav)" in the singular? Because Moses spoke from the inner perspective (milegav) while Jacob spoke from the outer perspective (milevar): regarding Jacob it is stated "grapes" in the plural, referring to the two great temptations and errors through which Hashem, blessed be He, would test and clarify the tribe of Judah—namely, the inclination for illicit relations (arayoit) and the inclination for idolatry (avodah zarah)—and Hashem, blessed be He, clarified that in its inner root Judah is pure of both;

וּמֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רָאָה כִּי אֵין לִיהוּדָא שׁוּם טָעוּת בְּיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כִּי בָּזֶה כְּבָר נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁהוּא נָקִי מְאֹד, רַק יִצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת צָרִיךְ עוֹד לְהִתְבָּרֵר,

whereas Moses spoke from the inner reality, for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, saw that inwardly Judah and Israel have no genuine attraction or error in the inclination for idolatry at all, since in that they were already clarified as completely pure, and only the single inclination for illicit desire ("the blood of the grape" in the singular) still required clarification—

כִּדְאָמַר רַב (סַנְהֶדְרִין סָמֶךְ גִּימֶל עַמּוּד בֵּית) "לֹא עָבְדוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הָעֵגֶל אֶלָּא לְהַתִּיר לָהֶם עֲרָיוֹת בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא" אֲבָל בְּיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּבָר הֵם נְקִיִּים וְהָבֵן.

as Rav stated in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 63b): "Israel did not worship idols (and the Golden Calf) except as a pretext to permit themselves forbidden relations in public," whereas regarding idolatry itself their hearts were already entirely free of it; understand this well.

p: בִּנְיָמִין זְאֵב יִטְרָף.
Benjamin is a wolf thatravens; in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at evening he shall divide the spoil.
כִּי בִּנְיָמִין הוּא מְקַבֵּץ כָּל הַטּוֹבוֹת מִבֵּין הָאוּמּוֹת וּמַכְנִיסָם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.

This means that Benjamin's spiritual power is to seize and gather in all the sparks of goodness and wealth swallowed up among the nations (as Mordechai and Esther took the house of Haman) and bring them into Israel.

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 7
p: גָּד גְּדוּד יְגוּדֶנּוּ וְהוּא יָגֻד עָקֵב.
Gad, a troop shall troop upon him, and he shall troop upon the heel.

דְּהִנֵּה בְּהַשְּׁנֵים עָשָׂר שִׁבְטֵי יָ"הּ נָתַן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אוֹר וְחַיִּים שֶׁאֵין אֶחָד דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵרוֹ, וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָאִים גְּבוּלֵי אֲלַכְסוֹן הַיְינוּ שֶׁאוֹרוֹ שֶׁל זֶה הוּא הֵיפֶךְ מִשֶּׁל זֶה,

For behold, within the twelve tribes of Yah the Holy One, blessed be He, implanted twelve distinct paths of light and vitality such that no one tribe resembles its fellow, and therefore they correspond to the twelve "diagonal boundaries" (gevulei alakhson, Sefer Yetzirah 5:2), meaning that the spiritual light of one is the converse of the other—
כִּי לָזֶה נִמְשָׁךְ כֹּחַ חִיּוּתוֹ מִמִּדַּת הָאַהֲבָה וְלָזֶה מִמִּדַּת הַיִּרְאָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה.
for one tribe draws the force of its vitality from the attribute of Love, while another draws from the attribute of Awe, and so forth.
וַעֲבוּר זֶה נִמְצָא כָּל הַפְּלוּגְתּוֹת בַּגְּמָרָא אַף כִּי הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם אֶחָד כְּדֵי לְקַיֵּים רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
And out of this diversity of soul-roots arise all the halakhic disputes in the Gemara, even though all of them are directed toward one single goal—to fulfill the will of Hashem, blessed be He,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצָאנוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (פְּסָחִים נּוּן גִּימֶל עַמּוּד בֵּית) "בֵּין שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְהַדְלִיק וּבֵין שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַדְלִיק שְׁנֵיהֶם לְדָבָר אֶחָד נִתְכַּוְּונוּ",
as we find in the Gemara (Pesachim 53b): "Whether those who said to light or those who said not to light, both intended one and the same purpose,"
וְכֵן הוּא כָּל הַפְּלוּגְתּוֹת כִּי מְקוֹרָם מִמָּקוֹם אֶחָד וְלָכֵן נִקְרָאִים שְׁבָטִים מִלְּשׁוֹן עֲנָפִים שֶׁמִּתְפַּשְּׁטִים לְכָאן וּלְכָאן.

and so it is with all authentic disputes of the Sages, for their source is from one unified root, which is why the tribes are called shevatim—from the expression of branches (shevet) that spread out in different directions from a single tree trunk.
וְהוּא שֶׁהִנִּיחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשֵׁבֶט גָּד מִדַּת יִסּוּרִין כִּי זֶה הַשֵּׁבֶט אוֹמֵר כִּי בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה בְּלֵב הָאָדָם בְּלֹא יִסּוּרִין,

Now Hashem, blessed be He, placed within the tribe of Gad the attribute of asceticism and affliction (yissurin), for this tribe's path maintains that it is impossible for words of Torah to penetrate a person's heart without afflictions and self-mortification;
וּבְדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם מִי שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל יִסּוּרִין אֵין לוֹ כָּל כָּךְ שִׂמְחָה וְאֵינוֹ כָּל כָּךְ בְּצַוְותָּא עִם בְּנֵי אָדָם.
yet in the natural way of the world, one who is given to afflictions and asceticism lacks joy and tends to withdraw from companionship and fellowship with other people.
וְלָכֵן נִתְבָּרְכוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם שִׂמְחָה וְצַוְותָּא, וּבֵרֵךְ אוֹתָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם הִתְחַבְּרוּת וְיִהְיֶה בָּהֶם גְּדוּדִים גְּדוּדִים,

Therefore Jacob blessed the tribe of Gad ("Gad, a troop shall troop upon him") that despite their rigorous path, they should be blessed with joy and fellowship (tzavta), uniting together in warm bands and fellowships (gedudim);
וְלָכֵן לֹא נִמְצָא בְּשׁוּם שֵׁבֶט שֶׁיִּכְלוֹל כָּל הַמִּסְפָּרִים הַיְינוּ מֵאוֹת וַאֲלָפִים וַעֲשָׂרוֹת רַק בְּשֵׁבֶט גָּד מַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ בִּשְׁאָר הַשְּׁבָטִים,

and for this reason, in the wilderness census (Numbers 1:25), Gad is the only tribe whose count includes thousands, hundreds, and tens (45,650)—signifying the harmonious binding together of all levels of society—unlike all the other tribes (whose counts end in round hundreds);

"וְהוּא יָגֻד עָקֵב" הַיְינוּ בִּזְמַן שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ לְקַבֵּץ אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אָז הוּא יֶאֱגוֹד וְיִקְשׁוֹר אֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּמִמֶּנּוּ יָבֹא כָּל מִינֵי שִׂמְחָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי אֵלִיָּהוּ הוּא מִשֵּׁבֶט גָּד כַּנִּזְכָּר בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עַיִן אָלֶף, יוֹד בֵּית).

"and he shall troop upon the heel (vehu yagud akev)" means that at the "heel" of time (the footsteps of the Messiah, ikvata d'meshicha), when it will be necessary to gather in all of Israel, he will bind and unite (ya'agod) all Israel together, and through him all manner of joy will come to Israel—for Elijah the Prophet, herald of the Redemption, stems from the tribe of Gad, as is mentioned in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 71:9).
h:
Gad and the Power to Overcome
For behold, within the twelve tribes of Yah the Holy One, blessed be He, implanted twelve distinct paths of light and vitality such that no one tribe resemb…

paras.r: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 8
p: נַפְתָּלִי אַיָּלָה שְׁלוּחָה הַנֹּתֵן אִמְרֵי שָׁפֶר.
Naphtali is a hind let loose; he gives goodly words.
הַיְינוּ כִּי נִמְצָא בּוֹ הַשָּׂגָה גְּדוֹלָה בְּכָל עִנְיְינֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לִשְׁאוֹל תֵּיכֶף מִי בָּרָא אֵלֶּה,
That is, within Naphtali resides a swift, keen perception regarding all the phenomena and fruits of this world to immediately look upward and ask, "Who created these?" (Isaiah 40:26);

וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "הַנֹּתֵן אִמְרֵי שָׁפֶר" הַיְינוּ שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁהָיָה מַכִּיר אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָל דָּבָר הָיָה נוֹתֵן הוֹדָאָה אֵלָיו, וְזֶה שֶׁתַּרְגּוּם אוּנְקְלוֹס יְהוֹן מוֹדִין וּמְבָרְכִין עֲלֵיהֶן.

and this is the meaning of "he gives goodly words"—that because he immediately recognized Hashem, blessed be He, in every enjoyment, he constantly offered thanksgiving and blessings to Him, as Onkelos translates: "they shall give thanks and bless over them."
